course.title: Data engineering: PostgreSQL, PostGIS, Redis and durable events
course.description: Understand service-owned data, forward migrations, spatial queries, cache correctness, outbox claims and recovery. Work with source-backed examples and disposable data instead of experimenting on production.

lessons.title: Design owned data and forward-only schema evolution
lessons.overview: PostgreSQL stores durable business facts; a schema change therefore affects more than a Java class. Begin with the owning service, the meaning of each fact, who may read or mutate it and whether older code must continue reading new rows. Academy is a useful contained example: its learner, progress, attempt, XP, activity, roadmap and audit data use the existing Auth database boundary. This course describes inspected source, not the current state of a live database. Do not infer that a migration is deployed merely because its SQL exists or a compile succeeded.

steps.label: Write a data dictionary
steps.detail: For every proposed column record meaning, type, nullability, owner, sensitivity, creation/update behavior and retention. Separate a domain identifier from an authentication identity, a client receipt from a business aggregate key, and a current status from a historical event. For money, preserve the owning domain's exact currency and amount representation; do not invent rounding rules.

steps.label: Read the actual constraints
steps.detail: Inspect services/auth-service/src/main/resources/db/migration/V7__craves_academy.sql in the repository and match it to AcademyService queries. Identify the owner/receipt keys, content-version progress keys and reward uniqueness. Constraints protect correctness when requests race; application validation alone is not equivalent. This historical path is a reading reference, not a file to edit after deployment.

steps.label: Plan additive evolution
steps.detail: A proposed new nullable field can often be introduced before all writers use it. Document the old-row behavior, any explicit backfill, reader compatibility and the point at which a constraint could safely tighten. Large backfills and indexes need separate execution plans and measured lock impact. Do not run an unbounded update in production as part of a training exercise.

steps.label: Keep applied migrations immutable
steps.detail: Inspect the current branch for duplicate or unused migration versions. Add a new migration rather than changing an applied SQL file or repairing Flyway history to conceal a mismatch. Record a migration's source, successful execution and resulting schema independently. A previous successful checksum is evidence to preserve, not a nuisance to remove.

steps.label: Prove transaction boundaries
steps.detail: An API may update several tables before returning. Test that a failure does not leave a partial durable state. The Academy persistence suite uses a disposable database and explicit transactions around directly constructed service calls. A rollback-compatible application release normally leaves additive data in place rather than dropping tables that contain learning history.

steps.label: Define evidence access
steps.detail: Use read-only, owner-scoped diagnostic queries where possible. Do not copy real customer, chef or learner rows into a public issue or a CI fixture. Report row counts and synthetic identifiers, with redacted evidence stored in an approved location. Schema access and production write approval remain separate permissions.

lessons.example: A new course version selects a new progress scope while historical XP remains in its separate ledger. An administrator may therefore see new assessment work without losing earned XP. Deleting old progress or ledger rows to make the dashboard look consistent would destroy evidence rather than solve versioning.
lessons.lab: In a disposable local PostgreSQL database, apply the existing Academy migration through the test setup and draw its key relationships. Predict the unique-key conflict for a duplicate owner/receipt and the result of an equivalent replay through the service. Draft an additive migration for the local-only bookmark exercise from the Java course, including old-row behavior and rollback compatibility; do not commit it to a production release. Record expected schema, actual schema, test results and cleanup of the disposable environment.
lessons.pitfall: Never equate a schema file in source control with deployed schema, and never edit successful Flyway history to hide a release error.

questions.prompt: A migration already succeeded in production. How should its behavior be corrected?
questions.explanation: Applied migrations remain immutable; corrections require explicit forward evolution and evidence.

questions.prompt: Why do unique constraints matter when application validation exists?
options: They protect invariants when concurrent requests race
questions.explanation: Database constraints provide a final concurrency-safe boundary for declared uniqueness.

questions.prompt: What should a code rollback normally do with additive Academy history?
options: Preserve the data and verify older-code compatibility
questions.explanation: Recovery should preserve durable evidence; destructive cleanup is not ordinary application rollback.

lessons.title: Keep spatial discovery and Redis caching correct
lessons.overview: Nearby discovery is a geographic query plus eligibility and privacy rules, not a simple text search. In the reviewed Catalog implementation, a request point is built with longitude followed by latitude, assigned SRID 4326 and cast to geography. Queries use ST_DWithin for a meter-based spatial filter and ST_Distance for ordering. The controller also composes a cache key from filters, paging, sorting and the privacy mode. Understand each dimension before adding an optimization. A faster answer is not useful if it comes from the wrong location, exposes private fields or serves an unavailable dish.

steps.label: Trace coordinates and units
steps.detail: Read REQUEST_LOCATION_CTE in NearbyDiscoveryService. The point construction order is longitude, latitude even though an API may list latitude first. Radius is expressed in meters in this contract. Use clearly labeled values in fixtures so an accidental swap or kilometer conversion error is detectable rather than hidden by a generous test radius.

steps.label: Separate eligibility from distance
steps.detail: The reviewed service applies active/available menu-item predicates and requires package metadata in its eligible-item logic. A kitchen being geographically nearby does not prove its menu is eligible or that a delivery provider can serve the order. Preserve domain-owned serviceability and package rules; training fixtures must not become default production radius policy.

steps.label: Inspect paging and ordering
steps.detail: Trace the sort and page/size parameters to the SQL. Test an empty result, equal-distance candidates, page boundaries and invalid parameters. If adding a tie-breaker or changing sort semantics, treat it as a contract change and test stable traversal rather than assuming the database returns a consistent order by itself.

steps.label: Read the full cache key
steps.detail: NearbyDiscoveryController includes resource type, privacyEnabled, coordinates, radius, text/category/dietary/price/preparation/spice filters, sort, page and size in the key. A new filter omitted from the key can mix results between different requests. Test that differing requests do not share an incorrect cached response.

steps.label: Prove invalidation and failure behavior
steps.detail: Inspect the actual cache service, enablement configuration, expiry and write-side invalidation before enabling it. A cache feature existing in source does not establish it is active in production. Test a changed availability value, cached empty result, Redis outage and privacy-mode change. Record the implemented fallback instead of assuming every Redis failure is harmless.

steps.label: Measure with representative synthetic data
steps.detail: Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) only on disposable read queries with representative rows and parameters; ANALYZE executes the query. Compare plans and latency before/after a proposed index. Do not claim a spatial index is used because one was created, and do not run expensive diagnostic queries on production without operational approval.

lessons.example: Two requests can share coordinates but use different dietary filters or privacy modes. Reusing one response for both would be a correctness or privacy defect. A cache-key test should vary one field at a time and prove that the returned data matches that request.
lessons.lab: Build a local fixture with a nearby eligible item, an unavailable item and a farther item. Trace the exact point construction, distance filter and eligibility predicates. Record query results with and without each filter and for two pages. In a local cache test, change one filter and then change availability; demonstrate request separation and the actual invalidation behavior. Keep all radii and coordinates explicitly labeled synthetic and do not turn on CRAVES_DISCOVERY_CACHE_ENABLED in a running service during this exercise.
lessons.pitfall: Redis is not the source of truth for order prices or payment state. Cache acceleration must preserve privacy, eligibility and historical correctness.

questions.prompt: What coordinate order does the reviewed ST_MakePoint expression use?
questions.explanation: The reviewed CTE passes longitude first, then latitude, before setting SRID and geography.

questions.prompt: A new discovery filter is added but omitted from the cache key. What is the risk?
options: Different requests may receive incorrectly shared results
questions.explanation: Cache identity must include request dimensions that affect the response.

options: Only prints hypothetical text without execution
Runs the query and reports observed execution information
questions.explanation: ANALYZE executes the query, so use approved environments and understand its operational cost.

lessons.title: Trace durable events through claims, retries and duplicate delivery
lessons.overview: A service cannot normally atomically commit its own PostgreSQL transaction and an unrelated provider or broker operation as one local database transaction. An outbox stores the intention to publish alongside the owning business change, then a worker delivers that intention. This reduces a failure gap but does not create magical exactly-once external effects. Craves OrderDomainOutboxRepository uses event-key uniqueness, bounded claims and lock tokens; its worker publishes allowed event types and records outcomes. Consumers and external commands still need their own duplicate and out-of-order protections.

steps.label: Trace the durable intention
steps.detail: Read the outbox insert and find its caller in the owning order transition. Confirm whether the domain write and outbox insert share the same transaction in that path. The repository's ON CONFLICT(event_key) DO NOTHING prevents duplicate event keys; it does not independently prove that every order transition is coupled atomically to event insertion.

steps.label: Understand bounded claiming
steps.detail: claimBatch selects eligible event types and retryable or stale-processing records with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then stamps PROCESSING, attempt count and a lock token. This lets workers avoid claiming the same available row simultaneously. Batch size, maximum attempts and stale-lock timing are engineering controls whose live values need separate inspection.

steps.label: Use claim ownership on completion
steps.detail: markPublished requires both the event ID and current lock token while the row is PROCESSING. An old worker must not finalize a claim another worker has recovered. The worker explicitly logs when a send succeeded but its claim was no longer current. Explain that state rather than treating it as a guaranteed unsent event.

steps.label: Model the send/ack gap
steps.detail: The broker can accept a message before the application records PUBLISHED. A crash or timeout in that gap can lead to another delivery attempt. Consumers must identify an already handled event and avoid repeating its business side effect. A booking or payment command needs its own durable idempotency and uncertain-outcome reconciliation.

steps.label: Keep retries bounded
steps.detail: The worker calculates bounded exponential retry delay and the repository moves exhausted attempts to DEAD. Do not reset attempts or requeue all dead records just to reduce a dashboard counter. Investigate the root cause and replay only an explicitly reviewed set with expected business effects and correlation evidence.

steps.label: Observe age and progress
steps.detail: Record oldest pending age, claim age, retries, dead records and successful progress, not only queue length. A queue with zero recent failures can still be stuck if its worker is disabled or no permitted event types are configured. Do not enable unrelated schedulers while deploying training content.

lessons.example: An event may have reached the broker even though the outbox row still appears PROCESSING. Blindly creating a new event with a new identity can bypass a consumer's duplicate detection. Preserve the original identity and reconcile the actual delivery outcome.
lessons.lab: In a disposable integration test, insert one synthetic outbox event twice and verify event-key uniqueness. Claim it with worker A, simulate a stale claim, recover it with worker B and prove that A cannot mark B's claim complete. Simulate a transport success followed by failure to record PUBLISHED and describe the required consumer replay protection. Record durable row states and effect counts, not just HTTP responses. No real Service Bus replay or provider call is permitted in this training exercise.
lessons.pitfall: An outbox is not proof of exactly-once execution. State the actual guarantees at the database, broker, consumer and provider boundaries separately.

questions.prompt: Why does markPublished check a claim token?
options: To prevent a stale worker from finalizing another worker's claim
questions.explanation: The token binds completion to the current claim owner.

questions.prompt: A broker accepted a message but the outbox update failed. What must be considered?
options: The message definitely was not sent
The event can be deleted safely
A later attempt may duplicate delivery and the consumer must handle it
questions.explanation: The send/acknowledgment gap makes duplicate delivery possible.

questions.prompt: What is the safe response to a dead-letter backlog?
options: Investigate and replay only an approved, reconciled set
questions.explanation: Bulk blind replay can repeat financial or delivery effects and destroy useful evidence.

lessons.title: Plan capacity, retention and recovery without making unsupported scale claims
lessons.overview: Capacity is a measured operating envelope, not a property obtained by choosing microservices, Redis or Kubernetes. Craves currently has an owner constraint to keep the relevant deployment at one replica; this training must not change it. Academy shares Auth's deployment and database boundary, so content reads, progress writes and activity heartbeats must remain bounded and must not degrade authentication. Database backups provide recovery options, while retention limits how long selected evidence is stored. Neither a configured backup policy nor a fast local query alone proves that a service can recover under a real incident.

steps.label: Identify resource budgets
steps.detail: List worker concurrency, database pool size, query duration, response body size, request rate, cache memory and outbound timeouts. For Academy, note the existing bounded source reads, catalog response limit in the BFF, per-learner write serialization and bounded activity credit. Verify actual configured values when releasing rather than copying historical assumptions.

steps.label: Measure load responsibly
steps.detail: Use a dedicated local or approved non-production environment with synthetic identities. Define requests per second, response-size distribution, concurrency and duration, then measure latency percentiles, errors, database waits and memory. Avoid a load generator pointed at live Auth, payment or delivery endpoints. A small smoke test is not load certification.

steps.label: Inspect expensive query shapes
steps.detail: Read AcademyService.state and analytics and identify how many rows and subqueries may be touched as learners grow. Use representative synthetic histories to test index behavior and pagination. Separate a possible future optimization from a guarantee already implemented. An existing LIMIT does not prove every count or subquery is inexpensive.

steps.label: Preserve retention semantics
steps.detail: Academy retains activity for 90 days and attempt receipts for 365 days while keeping progress and XP separately. Those are inspected implementation rules, not universal retention policy for Craves financial records. Test cleanup concurrency and old-data removal without deleting durable rewards. Do not apply Academy retention periods to orders, tax or settlement data.

steps.label: Distinguish backup configuration from restore proof
steps.detail: Before a real release, record the existing PostgreSQL backup/PITR configuration and a viable restore point. A recovery rehearsal requires an approved isolated target, which can create billable resources; training must stop before provisioning it. Verify restored schema and application reads before declaring a recovery drill successful.

steps.label: Write a reversible operating plan
steps.detail: Define which metric triggers a halt, which image is the rollback target, which additive data remains, and how to preserve the investigation record. Do not rotate working secrets, scale replicas, delete queues or redeploy unrelated services as a diagnostic shortcut. Obtain explicit approval for changes that increase cost or alter the deployment topology.

lessons.example: A larger curriculum can remain well below the BFF's one-MiB catalog response bound, but that does not demonstrate a million concurrent learners. Record serialized size and a measured load test separately from the functional count of lessons.
lessons.lab: Create a capacity worksheet for the Academy endpoints: read/write mix, response bytes, expected active learners, database operations, timeouts and current one-replica constraint. Run only a bounded local synthetic test and report what it did and did not measure. Produce a recovery worksheet with source/image/revision identifiers, backup evidence, application rollback and a separately approved restore rehearsal. Mark production load testing and restore provisioning NOT EXECUTED unless they were actually authorized and observed.
lessons.pitfall: Do not promise that a single replica supports one million concurrent users. Preserve current costs and report evidence-based limits and untested assumptions.

questions.prompt: What establishes a trustworthy capacity claim?
options: Representative measurements with a defined workload and limits
questions.explanation: Capacity claims require measured workload, resource and failure evidence.

questions.prompt: Does a configured PITR retention period prove a successful restore?
options: No; an isolated restore and application validation are separate evidence
Only if a course is completed
questions.explanation: Backup configuration and tested recoverability are distinct.

questions.prompt: May Academy's 90-day activity retention be applied to payment records automatically?
options: Yes, all data has the same policy
No; each domain needs its own approved retention policy
questions.explanation: Learning telemetry retention cannot silently replace financial or regulatory retention requirements.
